analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax limits that stop wealthy investors from deducting losses from passive investments.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let high-income investors deduct losses from businesses in which they don't actively work, was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1986, the tax code has barred people from using losses on 'passive' investments — businesses in which they invest money but don't materially work, such as real estate partnerships — to shelter their salaries or other active income from tax. This bill would repeal those limits entirely, effective for tax years after 1991, and undo related alternative-minimum-tax provisions. That would reopen a form of tax sheltering that the 1986 Tax Reform Act closed specifically to prevent high earners from avoiding tax on their actual income.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income individuals with passive investments — especially real estate investors and tax-shelter partnerships — would again be able to deduct paper losses from those ventures against their wages and business income, reducing or eliminating their tax on active earnings. Industry sponsors of passive investments would gain a renewed product to sell.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-income passive investors, especially in real estate

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 469 of the Internal Revenue Code, the rule that limits deductions of passive activity losses and credits, effective for tax years beginning after 1991.

The passive loss rules were enacted as part of the 1986 Tax Reform Act to stop taxpayers from using paper losses from investments they do not actively manage to shelter salaries and other active income.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall, meaning other taxpayers would shoulder a larger share of the tax burden, and the tax code would again allow sophisticated high earners to reduce tax on income from actual work through losses from investments they don't operate.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the passive loss limits would reduce federal revenue and shift more of the tax burden onto taxpayers without large passive investments, since someone has to make up the difference.

The limits exist to prevent tax avoidance; removing them would revive the tax-shelter structures the 1986 reform was designed to shut down, which critics at the time argued eroded the fairness and simplicity of the tax code.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow narrowly to high-income investors with passive holdings, while its costs — lost federal revenue and a reopened avoidance channel — fall broadly on other taxpayers. For ordinary working people, the drawbacks outweigh the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Ernest Hollings, joined by Sen. Trent Lott, introduced the bill on November 12, 1991.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no committee action, no report, and no floor vote after the referral, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers were better off, because the repeal that would have allowed high-income passive investors to shelter active income from tax never advanced; real estate and tax-shelter interests lost the chance at restored deductions.

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the passive activity loss limitations.

for.name: Sen. Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the repeal bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Daniel Patrick Moynihan (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote — letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but no votes were ever taken, so no party split shows in the record.

industries.note: The repeal would let these investors deduct paper losses from passive real estate holdings against wages and business income, restoring a major tax benefit. That gain comes at the cost of federal revenue borne by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Tax shelter and investment syndication promoters
industries.note: Repealing the passive loss rules would renew the market for tax-shelter products sold to high earners, a market the 1986 reform largely shut down. Ordinary taxpayers bear the lost revenue.
